reader.title: De Quincey railroad camp shooting
bases: Unknown gunmen fired more than fifty shots from the woods into a tent holding about twenty Black railroad workers, killing and wounding several, amid reported hostility to Black labor (A2, A5, A6).

Three independent dispatches (Beaumont A1, Lake Charles A3 and A6) and a New Orleans wire (A2, A5) agree that unknown persons fired into a tent of Black workers at De Quincey at night, killing at least one and wounding others.

summary.text: The De Quincey railroad camp shooting was a night attack on July 30, 1910, in which unknown gunmen fired into a tent of Black railroad workers at De Quincey, in Calcasieu Parish, Louisiana.
Will McMillin, a railroad employee, was killed outright and Susie Johnson was reported mortally wounded, while at least two others were hit; a New Orleans wire report counted two dead.
Papers linked the attack to local white hostility toward the railroad's use of Black labor, and the wire story was reprinted as far away as New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania.
De Quincey, a Frisco railroad shop town fifteen to twenty miles north of Lake Charles, housed Black laborers in a tent camp near the shops.

According to the New Orleans wire, there had been "much feeling" in the neighborhood, which it called "a white section," over the railroad's employment of Black workers, and a "similar shooting affray" had occurred some time before.
The Caucasian's Lake Charles dispatch said the trouble had been "brewing for some months," although it named the employer as the "Colorado Southern" railroad.
The Hattiesburg News added that a Frisco brakeman had beaten a white man a few days earlier, which some contended "may have fanned the flame of race feeling."
The Hattiesburg News placed the shooting on Saturday night, and a Beaumont dispatch dated July 31 said "last night."
The attackers fired from the surrounding woods and were not identified.
Most reports said about twenty Black men were in the tent and that more than fifty shots left it "riddled with bullets," while the Beaumont dispatch described three shotgun loads of buckshot.
Will McMillin, identified as a Black employee of the road, was killed instantly.
Susie Johnson was shot through the head and was not expected to live, and two other people in the tent were struck, one in the shoulder and one in the arm.
Officers from Lake Charles spent Sunday investigating the shooting, but no arrests had been made by August 2.
Some blamed a quarrel among the Black workers themselves, while others pointed to friction over Black labor in the Frisco shops.
A Louisiana news column in the Tensas Gazette on August 5 favored the second view, saying race feeling over Black labor "may be at the bottom of the affair."
No report of Johnson's death, an inquest, an arrest or a trial appears in the coverage.

The shooting reached print through three channels: a Beaumont dispatch in the Birmingham Age-Herald on August 1, Lake Charles dispatches in two Southern papers on August 2, and a New Orleans wire item carried mainly in the North.
The New York Sun ran the wire on August 2 under "Negroes Killed in Camp," and the Evening Journal printed it the same day as "Shoot Up Negro Camp," adding that "it is a wonder how any escaped."
The same paragraph reappeared on August 4 in the Monmouth Inquirer's roundup of "Crimes and Casualties" and on August 5 in the Honesdale Citizen.

In the South, the Age-Herald headed its brief "More Trouble for Negroes" and blamed "an unknown assassin," while the Caucasian, a Shreveport paper, used the headline "Black Killed Following Troubles."
The Hattiesburg News gave the fullest account under "Fusillade Poured Into Negro Tent," naming the victims and both theories of motive.
None of these white papers commented editorially, and the coverage includes no report from the Black press.

Accounts of the toll differed: the wire reported two killed and two seriously wounded, the Hattiesburg News one killed, one mortally wounded and two hurt, the Beaumont dispatch one killed, one wounded and a woman "perhaps fatally wounded," and the Caucasian one killed, a woman fatally wounded and "several negro men badly hurt."
The Hattiesburg special, the most detailed and the only one naming victims, lists one person killed outright.

Timing varied as well, since the Beaumont and Hattiesburg reports point to Saturday night, July 30, while the wire's "last night" from an August 1 dateline and the Caucasian's "early yesterday morning" point to July 31.
The Caucasian alone named the employer as the Colorado Southern; every other account said the Frisco.

accounts.label: Beaumont dispatch
accounts.gist: One Black man killed and another wounded and a woman perhaps fatally wounded when three buckshot loads were fired into a tent on the Frisco railroad from the darkness by 'an unknown assassin'; no clue.

accounts.label: New Orleans wire report
accounts.gist: Unknown parties fired more than fifty shots from the woods into a tent of twenty Black Frisco workers, killing two and seriously wounding two; there had been much feeling in the white neighborhood over Black labor and an earlier similar shooting.

accounts.label: Lake Charles dispatch (Shreveport Caucasian)
accounts.gist: After months of trouble over Black labor employed by the 'Colorado Southern' railroad, workers at the De Quincey car shops were fired on early in the morning; one killed, a woman fatally wounded, several men badly hurt.

accounts.label: Lake Charles special (Hattiesburg News)
accounts.gist: More than fifty shots fired from ambush on Saturday night killed Will McMillin and mortally wounded Susie Johnson and hit two others; Lake Charles officers investigated without arrests; motive attributed either to a quarrel among the Black workers or to friction over Black labor.

framing.detail: The Sun ('Negroes Killed in Camp') and Evening Journal ('Shoot Up Negro Camp') ran the New Orleans wire, which explained the attack by local 'feeling' over Black labor in 'a white section'.

The Age-Herald headed its brief 'More Trouble for Negroes' and blamed 'an unknown assassin'; the Caucasian headed its item 'Black Killed Following Troubles' and tied it to months of trouble over Black labor.
The Hattiesburg News ('Fusillade Poured Into Negro Tent') named the victims and set out two theories, a quarrel among the Black workers or race feeling over Black labor.
The Tensas Gazette's Louisiana news column gave one sentence, suggesting race feeling over Black labor in the Frisco shops was 'at the bottom of the affair'.
